Stephen King’s literary works have birthed some of the most iconic horror masterpieces in cinema history. However, the 1983 film adaptation of Cujo represents a staggering failure in narrative execution, stands as a masterclass in bad screenplaying, and serves as an ultimate waste of audience time. What promises to be a tense, claustrophobic thriller quickly devolves into an exercise in narrative stupidity, structural overkill, and profound boredom. The primary catalyst for the film's failure is the sheer stupidity woven into the fabric of the screenplay. For a horror film to maintain tension, the characters must make choices that feel organic, even if desperate. In Cujo, the characters are driven entirely by contrived ignorance designed solely to force the plot forward. The screenplay relies on a series of absurdly convenient oversights: a breaking car that happens to fail at the worst possible location, characters who refuse to communicate basic information to one another, and a complete lack of survival instincts. Because the script fails to establish intelligent stakes, the audience is left rooting against the human protagonists rather than fearing the antagonist. This structural ineptitude leads directly into the film's most egregious flaw: the central conflict gets boring after exactly five minutes. The novelty of a rabid St. Bernard trapping a mother and child inside a sweltering Ford Pinto wears off almost immediately. Once the physical parameters of the siege are established, the film completely runs out of ideas. The audience is subjected to endless, repetitive cycles of the dog barking at the window, the characters screaming, and the dog retreating, only to repeat the sequence moments later. Stripped of psychological depth or escalating tension, the film ceases to be scary and becomes aggressively monotonous. Compounding this boredom is the screenplay's reliance on overkill. Lacking the nuance required to sustain a feature-length film in a single location, the filmmakers substitute genuine terror with relentless, loud overstimulation. The editing becomes frantic, the score shrieks at every minor movement, and the dog is subjected to an absurd amount of cosmetic gore that feels cartoonish rather than frightening. By dialing every sensory element up to eleven without any narrative progression, the film numbs the audience. The overkill exposes the fundamental emptiness of the script; it is a short story stretched violently beyond its breaking point. Cujo is a monumental waste of time. It takes a terrifying, subtext-rich novel about family fractures and domestic terror and flattens it into a dull, repetitive creature feature. The screenplay lacks the wit to engage the mind, the pacing to hold the attention, or the restraint to build actual dread. Instead of delivering a tight, memorable thriller, Cujo leaves its audience trapped in a stagnant vehicle of poor filmmaking, praying for the credits to roll.

Cujo es una crítica a nuestra sociedad actual. El perro constantemente queda en segundo plano para que nos enfoquemos en las dinámicas familiares que se nos muestran en la película, como lo son las familias de Vic y Joe. Por un lado tenemos la infidelidad de Donna y por el otro el maltrato que Joe ejerce sobre Charity. Con esto claro, puedo ver que la película no quiere enseñarnos la historia de un perro asesino infestado de rabia; quiere mostrarnos cómo este tipo de dinámicas tóxicas afectan a los miembros más vulnerables de la familia; como a los hijos, por ejemplo. Ahora, sinceramente esto me lo saqué del fundillo. Yo sí quería ver una película de un perro asesino infestado de rabia, joder, si quisiera ver una película de drama familiar, pues simplemente miraría una de drama familiar, pero este no es el caso. Joder, yo quería mi película de terror, carajo, odio como dejaron al puto perro en segundo plano solo para enfocarse en las misms problemáticas familiares que mencioné solo para burlarme. La próxima vez, si haces una película que a penas trata sobre un perro asesino, no pongas su nombre como título; algunos nos podemos llevar una gran decepción.

Cujo ist einer der langweiligsten Filme, die ich jemals gesehen habe. Ich habe generell große Probleme mit dem Subgenre des Tierhorrorfilms. Vor allem bei denen, die sich selbst ernst nehmen. Für mich funktioniert das einfach nicht, weil der Suspension-of-Disbelief-Faktor astronomisch hoch ist. Gerade in Cujo müssen wir so viele Logiklöcher akzeptieren und wir werden völlig realitätsbefreiten Tierverhalten ausgesetzt, es bricht sämtliche Immersion. Und das alles wäre schon schlimm genug, hinzu kommt allerdings noch, dass Cujo ein grauenhaft langsames Erzähltempo hat, einen völlig unpassendes Disney-Heideldei-Score und weil der Regisseur nach Produktionsbeginn ausgetauscht wurde, gibt es ein paar lose Enden in der Handlung, die nie auserzählt werden. Das erste Drittel des Films funktioniert noch, da ist Cujo primär ein Familiendrama, sobald der mordhungrige Hund die Bühne betritt, verliert der Film aber sämtliche Originalität, Raffinesse und Spannung. Eine Mutter und ihr Sohn schwitzen sich in einem Auto zutode, weil sie von einem Berhardiner belagert werden – und ja: Es ist genau so dumm, wie es sich anhört. Ich will hier nicht Spoilern, aber ich sage so viel: Stephen King schrieb dieses Buch auf dem Höhepunkt seiner Drogenabhängigkeit. Laut eigenen Aussagen kann er sich kaum noch daran erinnern Cujo geschrieben zu haben. Das erklärt für mich den völlig bescheuerten dritten Akt. Cujo ist ein absoluter Schnarcher, ein Creature-Feature-B-Movie, ich vergebe 3,8 von 10 Punkten.

This was not great. A hard thing when adapting books to the screen is capturing all that rich internal narrative. Even with human characters, it can be hard to cram all of those thoughts onto the screen in a way that doesn’t feel forced. When the character is a dog, however, it is a much more difficult feat. And here, it shows. The book is full of Cujo’s own thoughts and feelings about what is happening to him. How he is reacting to sights and sounds once the rabies takes hold of him. It’s obviously incredibly hard to do this on screen, so we don’t get any of that. We’re also missing lots of important information about characters that we learn in the book. Lots of background and context for why they act the way they do. I get stuff has to be cut to account for a reasonable run time, but so much was cut here. Performances were decent, I don’t think anyone stood out in particular apart from the dog playing Cujo. Some parts of the plot were changed, and I don’t think they worked particularly well. Overall, quite disappointed with this considering how much I enjoyed the book!

Wenn die Langeweile zur Last wird. Um das direkt zu Beginn klar zu stellen: Ich bin kein großer Fan der Buchvorlage von Stephen King, aber dennoch habe ich versucht dem Film eine faire Chance zu geben. Allerdings ist dieser Film so hochgradig langweilig, dass mir das irgendwann einfach nicht mehr möglich war. Denn die Geschichte zieht sich und zieht sich und es hört nicht auf. Sekunden werden zu Minuten, Minuten zu Stunden. Und dann sitzt da dieser Hund vor dem kaputten Auto, in welchem eine Mutter mit ihrem Kleinkind sitzt und es passiert nichts. Selbst wenn der Hund angreift ist das kaum spannend genug, um die Minuten davor und danach noch zu retten. Ich saß knappe 90 Minuten da und habe mir eine Film angesehen, der sich wie 180 anfühlt und versucht, den Zuschauer durch die Langeweile zu erdrücken. Die Handlung fand ich im Buch schon nicht allzu spannend. Vor allem aber auch, da ein Gefühl aufgebaut wird, welches mir nicht gefällt. Dieser Zeitdruck, der geschaffen wird, da die beiden Festsitzenden langsam einfach nicht mehr durchhalten. Im Film war das auch der Fall, aber es war mir ab einem gewissen Punkt einfach egal. Ich wusste was passieren würde, auch wenn der Film in einem Fall den Schwanz einzieht, und dann war es eben so. Die Handlung hat mich einfach kalt gelassen. Den Punkt, den ich "Cujo" aber geben muss, ist der Look und die Inszenierung. Denn der Look hat mich immer wieder an Horrorfilme aus den 70ern erinnert, die einfach dreckig und räudig aussehen. Genau das schafft der Film auch hin und wieder, was mir ziemlich gut gefallen hat. Die Inszenierung ist ebenfalls nicht übel. Diese beiden Punkt habe ich dann doch noch neutral sehen können. Denn das muss ich einfach sagen. Der Film scheitert an der Prämisse und nicht an der technischen Umsetzung, da ich die Kamera und Inszenierung vollkommen solide fand. Insgesamt ist "Cujo" also ein Film, den ich aufgrund des Pacings ziemlich schwer zu ertragen fand. 2/5 Sternen.

A snoozer of a King adaptation as horror that does have a couple things going for it as a family drama. Danny Pintauro is fantastic in his role as little Tad, making me believe he was actually frightened for his life when he and his mom were stuck in the car with zombified Cujo stalking outside (the best part of the whole movie by a mile). I've also got to give the film credit for its portrayal of the male lead as a father. It's rare to see good dads in movies that aren't explicitly geared as family fare. Dee Wallace's mom character is portrayed far more negatively, the way dads are more often shown, and the script lets her contain multitudes, as she seeks selfish pleasure and ultimately protects her son when she has to. It's pretty refreshing, actually. Cujo himself is a menacing villain, but everything plays out in such a lazy, laconic way that your interest flags. It's also shot with zero panache. Passable in ways, but it lacks the humor of better adaptations like Graveyard Shift and the pure filmmaking muscle of ones like Christine .

Cujo is one of those stories that necessarily works better as a book than a movie because so much of the "action" takes place in the characters' minds. When it's translated to film, it's just not that interesting to watch two people sit in a car for an extended period of time—even if that car is a Pinto. Donna (Dee Wallace) and Vic Trenton (Daniel Hugh Kelly) are a seemingly happily married couple, although Donna is having an affair with the local "stud," Steve Kemp (Christopher Stone). Also, the Trentons' son Tad (Danny Pintauro) is having nightmares about a monster in his closet. Meanwhile, Vic's car has been having some problems, and the local garage is overloaded with customers. The mailman tells Vic that a local guy, Joe Camber (Ed Lauter), will fix his car, and "won't charge you an arm-and-a-leg for it, either." Vic, Donna, and Tad take a drive out to see Joe—and that's where they meet Cujo. Cujo is a happy-go-lucky St. Bernard. What no one knows is that Cujo, unfortunately, was bitten on the nose by a rabid bat. A few days later, Vic leaves on a ten-day business trip. Donna and Tad take her misbehaving Pinto out to Joe's place—but unbeknownst to them, Cujo has gone full-blown rabid! He's now a killer! He's also really, really dirty. Yuck! Everything about Cujo feels very TV movie-ish to me, from the screenwriting to the editing to the music. If it weren't for a few profanities and some gore, this could very easily have been the ABC Sunday Night Movie. And if it had been a made-for-TV movie, it would have been pretty good. As a feature film, however, it's not too engaging. It's the type of film where you can't help but think, If I were in Donna's shoes, I would be making different choices. I don't think I would sit in my Pinto for hours on end.

When I think of Cujo, one of the first things that comes to mind is what Stephen King once said about the novel: he doesn’t remember writing it. King penned the book while struggling with alcoholism and later admitted that he had no real awareness of the process—he just knew the story came out well and became a huge success. The film adaptation, released in August 1983, didn’t fare as well with critics but was a box office hit. Cujo tells the story of a friendly Saint Bernard who becomes rabid after being bitten by a bat. Donna Trenton (Dee Wallace) has recently separated from her husband following the revelation of an affair. Her five-year-old son, Tad (Danny Pintauro), adores the dog, whose owners—young Brett Camber (Billy Jayne) and his father, a mechanic (Ed Lauter)—don’t mind the visits. One day, Donna and Tad come to see Cujo only to discover that the dog has turned into a violent killing machine and has already attacked one of his owners. When their car dies and they are trapped inside under the summer sun, Cujo’s aggression escalates, and the two must figure out a way to survive with no help in sight. I last watched this film sixteen years ago, and my opinion hasn’t changed. The story is solid, and there are genuinely suspenseful moments, but the pacing drags. The majority of the action takes place in a single location, and the ending is easy to predict. That said, the film is effective in its tension-building, with Cujo appearing suddenly to deliver moments of real terror. The script provides some character development, but the slow progression makes the experience feel longer than it really is. I also read Cujo in high school and, as often happens, the book outshines the film. The novel’s suspense and depth are far superior to the movie, though the adaptation does capture certain frightening moments and presents them in a realistic, well-executed way. Cujo himself is genuinely terrifying at times, and the film does have moments that will make your heart race. Ultimately, while the movie has its merits, it’s a slow burn that doesn’t fully live up to the tension and richness of King’s original story.

In the words of Rachel Greene, “What is wrong with that dog?!?” It’s a very faithful adaptation of the book even with having to slim down on the story and scenes with the wife and son of the mechanic and some of the stuff with the Vic Trenton regarding the Sharpe account that was in the book. But all the elements are there that contribute to Donna and Tad being trapped in the car while being terrorized by Cujo who’s been infected with rabies. Absolutely insane how far they went with certain aspects of that last third to show the slow terror of being trapped in the car by an animal who wants to bite you and kill you. Same with how vicious they let Cujo be and visceral it was to see him bite Donna - same with how gross and bloody he becomes by the end of the film. Another thing I liked with the second to last confrontation between Cujo and Donna was how they used the camera to approach Donna like it was Cujo even moving like the diseased dog to get the effect. Just a good move to get the terror of the situation across without having to show the dog being hit by the baseball bat in the process. One thing I didn’t like about the film was that it chickened out on the ending of the book where Tad dies. Obviously, it’s sad and meant to break you emotionally for what both of the characters went through only to be futile in the end, but it fits with the message of the book that King wrote out in that things can happen beyond your control and that you have to learn to live with it rather than just shove it under the rug. It still could have fit in the movie given that it followed the beats of the plot of the book. Maybe in 1983 it was just too much of a downer or maybe the film didn’t have the budget to have the police and ambulance arrive to a Donna who was trying to resuscitate her son for so long after killing Cujo. I can’t say for certain, but it’s my one disappointment in the movie since it was faithful up until that point.

This adaptation derives its horror from the systematic collapse of domestic security. Rather than presenting evil as an external or supernatural force, the film finds violence within the familiar, transforming the family dog into an agent of biological disorder. Cujo’s descent into rabies is consequently devoid of moral purpose - his violence is pathological, arbitrary and indifferent to human suffering. Dee Wallace gives a notable performance, gradually moving from domestic anxiety towards states of acute psychological and physical distress. Pintauro’s presence intensifies the film’s emphasis on vulnerability and dependence. Teague’s direction is similarly restrained, employing increasingly claustrophobic compositions and restricting movement as the narrative progresses. The automobile becomes both shelter and prison, while heat, dehydration and mechanical failure function as additional instruments of physical deterioration. The film’s fairly austere tone derives from this refusal of melodrama - as Cujo presents terror as a material condition, in which ordinary structures of safety prove temporary, unreliable and ultimately incapable of containing violence. CUJO Kritik Review (1983): Cujo ist ein Horrorfilm, Thriller und Survival-Horror mit Mystery- und Monsterfilm-Elementen und basiert auf Stephen Kings gleichnamigem Roman. Lewis Teagues Verfilmung erzählt von dem zunächst freundlichen Bernhardiner Cujo, der nach einem Fledermausbiss an Tollwut erkrankt und zu einer tödlichen Bedrohung wird. Im Mittelpunkt stehen Donna Trenton und ihr Sohn Tad, die während einer Autopanne auf dem Grundstück der Cambers in ihrem Wagen festsitzen und von Cujo belagert werden. Die größte Stärke des Films ist seine beklemmende Atmosphäre. Cujo braucht erstaunlich wenig klassische Horroreffekte, um Spannung aufzubauen. Besonders die Hitze, die Enge des Autos und das Wissen, dass der Hund jederzeit angreifen könnte, erzeugen ein starkes Gefühl der Ausweglosigkeit. Die scheinbar alltägliche Situation entwickelt sich dadurch langsam zu einem echten Überlebenskampf. Auch Dee Wallace überzeugt als Donna. Sie vermittelt glaubwürdig die zunehmende Panik und Verzweiflung einer Mutter, die nicht nur um ihr eigenes Leben, sondern vor allem um das ihres Kindes kämpfen muss. Danny Pintauro funktioniert ebenfalls gut als Tad, dessen Angst die ohnehin angespannte Situation zusätzlich verstärkt. Besonders interessant ist, dass der Film sich zunächst viel Zeit für das Familiendrama nimmt. Die Eheprobleme zwischen Donna und Vic sowie Donnas Affäre wirken zunächst fast wie eine völlig andere Geschichte. Dadurch entsteht allerdings ein Kontrast zum späteren Horror: Die privaten Probleme werden zunehmend unwichtig, sobald Donna und Tad tatsächlich ums Überleben kämpfen müssen. Cujo selbst ist eine überraschend effektive Horrorfigur. Der Film macht aus ihm kein übernatürliches Monster, sondern einen durch Tollwut gefährlich gewordenen Hund. Gerade diese Bodenständigkeit macht die Bedrohung glaubwürdiger. Der Horror funktioniert dadurch weniger wie Fantasy und stärker wie ein realistischer Survival-Thriller. Auch die Inszenierung von Lewis Teague kann überzeugen. Die Kamera nutzt besonders das Auto als klaustrophobischen Schauplatz und macht aus einem eigentlich kleinen Raum eine zunehmend unerträgliche Falle. Die begrenzte Bewegungsfreiheit der Figuren wird dabei konsequent für die Spannung genutzt. Das größte Problem liegt für mich im langen Aufbau. Der Film braucht relativ viel Zeit, bevor Cujo tatsächlich zur zentralen Bedrohung wird. Das Familiendrama besitzt zwar seine Berechtigung, wirkt aber stellenweise etwas zu ausführlich. Wer hauptsächlich einen Tierhorrorfilm erwartet, muss entsprechend Geduld mitbringen. Auch die Nebenfiguren bleiben teilweise oberflächlich. Einige Handlungsstränge rund um die Familie Camber und Donnas Eheprobleme tragen zwar zur Ausgangssituation bei, erhalten aber nicht immer genügend Tiefe, um wirklich interessant zu werden. Die Horror-Sequenzen selbst sind dafür deutlich stärker. Sobald Donna und Tad im Auto festsitzen, entwickelt Cujo eine wesentlich intensivere Dynamik. Die wiederholten Angriffe könnten leicht eintönig wirken, doch die zunehmende körperliche Erschöpfung und die Hitze sorgen dafür, dass sich die Situation immer weiter zuspitzt. Visuell ist der Film für seine Zeit ordentlich umgesetzt. Die Aufnahmen von Cujo funktionieren vor allem deshalb gut, weil die Inszenierung nicht permanent versucht, ihn spektakulär aussehen zu lassen. Stattdessen reicht häufig schon seine Präsenz vor dem Auto aus, um Spannung zu erzeugen. Auch die vergleichsweise zurückhaltende Darstellung von Gewalt unterstützt den realistischen Ton. Das Erzähltempo ist insgesamt etwas unausgewogen. Die erste Hälfte ist deutlich ruhiger und stärker vom Familiendrama geprägt, während die zweite Hälfte wesentlich konzentrierter auf den Überlebenskampf setzt. Dadurch fühlt sich der Film fast wie zwei unterschiedliche Geschichten an, die erst später vollständig zusammenfinden. Das Finale liefert schließlich einen intensiven Überlebenskampf und funktioniert emotional vor allem durch Donnas Entschlossenheit, ihren Sohn zu retten. Die Auflösung ist wirkungsvoll, auch wenn sie gegenüber Stephen Kings Roman verändert wurde. Fazit: Cujo ist ein atmosphärischer und teilweise sehr spannender Tierhorrorfilm, der besonders durch seine realistische Bedrohung, die klaustrophobische Auto-Situation und Dee Wallaces starke Darstellung überzeugt. Der lange Aufbau, das teilweise ausgedehnte Familiendrama und einige oberflächliche Nebenfiguren verhindern für mich eine höhere Bewertung. Sobald der eigentliche Überlebenskampf beginnt, zeigt der Film jedoch deutlich, warum er zu den bekannten Stephen-King-Verfilmungen der 1980er gehört.

Cujo ist zur Hälfte ein Ehedrama: Ganz im Stile Stephen Kings ist das Vorstandleben nicht ganz die Idylle, die es vorgibt zu sein. Die Frau hat ne Affäre und der Mann verdient die Brötchen - passend zum nur scheinbar perfekten Eheleben - damit, den Menschen mit seinen Werbespots Froot Loops als gesundes Frühstück aufzutischen. Parallel dazu gibt's noch einen Automechaniker, der auch nicht gerade eine liebevolle Beziehung zu seiner Frau zu führen scheint. Und dann ist da noch dieser riesige Bernhardiner, dem nach einem Fledermausbiss die Sabber nur so aus dem Mund läuft. Nach einer Menge Build Up wird Cujo ungefähr ab der Hälfte zu dem Tierhorrorfilm, den der Titel verspricht. Als solcher ist er recht effektiv, auch wenn nicht viel passiert. Die Protagonisten schmoren die meiste Zeit im Auto. Man kann sich genau vorstellen, wie ein ähnliches Konzept heute noch mit der einen oder anderen zeitgenössischen Drehbuchuidee ausgeschmückt würde, um das Publikum bei Laune zu halten. Ich erinnere nur mal an das bekloppte Fortnite-Finale von "Unhinged", in dem Russell Crowe in der Rolle des tollwütigen Bernhardiners zu sehen war. Cujo hätten zumindest ein paar mehr Ideen auch nicht geschadet, dafür knocked es Kameramann Jan de Bont bei nahezu jeder Gelegenheit out of the park. Die Schauspieler sind auch top und der Hund ist ein Feini. Da lässt sich letztlich verschmerzen, dass die beiden Hälften des Films sich nicht wirklich zu einem stimmungsvollen Ganzen vereinen.

In what many have called Dee Wallace's best performance in a film, "Cujo" was her moment to shine.  Dee Wallace is most proud of this film and Stephen King himself has stated that he loved her portrayal in this one above any others from his adaptive works.  It is easy to see why.  This was not an easy part to fill.  It was grueling, and very hard on her physically and mentally, but the results are clear.  This is one of those personal favorites that I've seen many times over the years, and it never gets old for me. Vic and Donna are a couple with a young son named Tad who bravely goes to bed every night afraid that the monster in his closet will get him.  The marriage is in a fragile place when it is discovered that Donna has been having an affair.  Vic uses a business trip to think things over and leaves for a week.  While he is gone, Donna drives her ailing car out to the Camber farm where they've had engine work done before.  She takes Tad with her.  However, when they arrive, they find that nobody is home except for their overly large St. Bernard dog, Cujo, who has gone rabid.  With the car sitting dead and nobody in sight, it becomes a grueling game of survival - not only against Cujo, but against the elements as well. As with all Stephen King stories, the characters are always well fleshed out, deep and rich.  The story was well developed with excellent pacing, and the visuals are memorable.  The opening scene with the camera following the rabbit couldn't have been easy to capture on film.  This wasn't CGI or AI here.  That was the real thing.  The work that both Dee Wallace and Danny Pintauro had to put in was nothing short of inspiring.  Some feel that Dee Wallace should've gotten a nod at award nomination time and was snubbed - the reason being was that this was a horror film. The work that was done with the different St. Bernard's with the training and filming was also outstanding.  Apparently, 13 different dogs were used throughout the film to get the results they were looking for.  The mood and atmosphere is set early, and holds true to the very end.  I've always loved this movie.  Other than the acting, I don't think this is one of the better King adaptations, but it is a good one.  I would highly recommend it to anyone who hasn't seen it yet.  It will make you appreciate having a car that is reliable and runs good - that is for sure!

Hay que poseer una mente muy enferma y retorcida para concebir una historia como "Cujo"...por fortuna este es el mayor don de Stephen King, quien además lo combinó con intensas dosis de alcohol mientras lo escribía, razón por la que hoy no recuerda casi nada de aquel proceso. El asesinato de un niño por un san bernardo en Maine o aquel día que llevó a arreglar su moto y fue atacado por un perro de la misma raza pudo servirle de inspiración, si bien por aquellas fechas ya se estrenaron algunas películas donde el llamado "mejor amigo del hombre" era convertido en su peor asesino...pero el poder de "Cujo" es mucho más fascinante, también uno de los relatos de horror más descarnadamente tristes que se hayan escrito, por lo creíble de la presencia del Mal y por explorar el miedo interior de un animal a perder su alma debido a un elemento sobrenatural que no entiende del todo (una infección en este caso). El pasaje donde mejor se expresa esto es cuando Cujo emerge cual espectro de un banco de neblina al notar la presencia del "Chico" (Brett); en otro tiempo su más fiel compañero, pero ahora su incontrolable furor asesino le incita a "echarse sobre él, desgarrarle y beber su sangre"...hasta que escucha su voz de nuevo y le reconoce ("Es "el Chico", y "el Chico" nunca le había hecho daño"). En recomendación del propio King, Lewis Teague, director de "La Bestia bajo el Asfalto" y "The Lady in Red", fue contratado como reemplazo de Peter Medak para la adaptación, que llegó dos años y muchos elogios después (amén de críticas negativas). Pero aquí, aunque la trama se sigue más o menos igual, se cometen dos errores clave: uno es que el ataque del murciélago que infecta a Cujo se produce al empezar la película, mientras en el libro la familia Trenton se cruza con él antes, por lo tanto es más comprensible y también menos sutil el terror que el perro infunde a Donna. Su álter-ego literario siente el miedo como un inexplicable presagio del caos que surgirá tras una conjunción de sucesos fortuitos; esta sensación casi crea una atmósfera onírica en el libro (y es que al principio se recuerda al asesino Frank Dodd, personaje de "The Dead Zone" que simboliza el Mal, un Mal con muchas caras, un Mal que aparece de cuando en cuando y es auténtico). En el film todos estos bonitos detalles no existen porque la versión de Cronenberg se estaba rodando en ese momento y porque, sinceramente, habría quedado muy ridículo en pantalla escuchar los pensamientos de Cujo con voz "en off"; el guión mantiene la infidelidad de Donna y las ganas de huir de Charity, esposa del tipo que arregla el coche de los Trenton, y así, una vez más, las familias disfuncionales, sin importar la clase a la que pertenecen, son parte del universo "kingniano", o parte del poco atractivo ambiente de Maine. En el primer caso la mujer produce repulsión, en el segundo lástima, aunque los abusos físicos a Charity no se muestran aquí, pero no hay que ser muy listo para saber que suceden casi todos los días. Este malestar familiar, lejos de ser gratuito, ayuda a que el futuro desastre se produzca, y a eso se unen problemas tan reales y cotidianos, como estropearse un coche, que parecieran maquinados por algún ente despiadado del lugar; Teague y el director de fotografía Jan de Bont, con mucho esmero por el aspecto visual, saben imprimir de algún modo mágico esta sensación de horror latente a las atmósferas (sobre todo en la secuencia donde Cujo, como en el libro, surge de la espesa niebla ante Brett) antes de dejarnos atrapados igual que a Donna y al pequeño Tad dentro del viejo Ford Pinto en el patio de Joe. La siguiente 2.ª parte de la historia ya se olvida de Charity y su hijo (en las páginas no sucedía) y casi de Vic para centrarse en el calvario, inimaginable, que vivirán ellos dos, y esto es un "tour de force", un desesperante torbellino de tensión iniciado con el pasmoso y memorable salto que pega el animal sobre el coche de la mujer. El lector no podrá olvidar la descripción del mejor encuentro entre Donna y Cujo en el libro, con ese colorido uso de la prosa adjetival que sólo King tiene ("Los ojos del perro se posaron en ella, estaban colorados y legañosos, y de ellos goteaba una especie de sustancia viscosa; el perro parecía derramar lágrimas pegajosas y su pelo estaba cubierto de barro...¡y sangre, es eso, es sangre, Dios santo!"). Pero la pericia de Teague y los buenos efectos especiales consiguen su propósito, y por supuesto las sorprendentes interpretaciones del pequeño Danny Pintuaro y Dee Wallace, metidos a conciencia en los personajes y en el abismo infernal al que han ido a parar por casualidad. La de Donna es una lucha con importantes subtextos: destruir por cuestión de supervivencia la naturaleza que el ser humano aparentemente creía poder domesticar y la creencia en el Mal como algo plausible, real, de carne y hueso. Bueno, es imposible igualar la pesadilla que suscitan las páginas... Pero el director te absorbe con esa fuerza visceral y sabe ponerte en el lugar de Donna, en ese Pinto abrasado por el sol del verano más caluroso de Maine, reflexionando sobre la cuestión de que hay que matar y destruir para proteger lo que queremos; por desgracia el film no puede permitirse ser todo lo pesimista que fue el autor en su conclusión (lo que llevó su libro, entre otras cosas, a una fuerte controversia). No es tan creíble ni tan poderoso, es más bien una solución al estilo hollywoodiense, nada propia para el aluvión de brutalidad que se nos ha echado encima en unos minutos. Los personajes de King no tenían el control del destino ni de la naturaleza en sus manos, así como el conejo que se escondió en la madriguera no tuvo más remedio que morir de hambre miserablemente por el Mal que permanecía fuera. El guión no llega a estas conclusiones tan devastadoras, claro...

I probably hadn’t seen this movie since the Blockbuster Video days of the mid-to-late 90’s, when it would be one of a stack of weekend VHS offerings for my newlywed wife and I.  Recently my 11-year old suggested it for our ongoing exploration of horror movies, based on my fond memories. At first, I was afraid it wasn’t going to live up to my memory of it; a slow-burn build is expected for any good Stephen King story, but Cujo flirts with movie-of-the-week vibes really early. Heavy handed scoring, paint-by-numbers editing, and two underplayed leads that feel more like they’re in an 80s network TV show. Dee Wallace and Daniel Hugh Kelly just feel kind of…light. The time taken ends up serving the story, though,  because once the match is struck, this film ignites and completely explodes . The sequence trapped in the car is outright terrifying , not only for the brilliantly constructed jumpscares and heart thumping suspense buildup, but also for the visceral authenticity of Wallace and 7-year old Danny Pintauro. (Pintauro, in particular, is the heart of the film. How a child that age could so realistically portray terror is beyond me. I wonder if the poor kid actually was traumatized.) Totally deserving of its status as a classic 80s horror film, truly scary, and a welcome respite from the tongue-in-cheek slasher offerings of the era. The only thing that puts it a notch or two under Misery is the lack of Caan and Bates. If you’ve never seen it, treat yourself. (Just suffer through the first twenty minutes.)

É impressionante que, na época em que escreveu e lançou o livro homônimo, em 1981, Stephen King passava pelo pior momento de sua vida, quando estava viciado em álcool e cocaína. Por causa disso, o autor não se lembrava de ter escrito Cujo. Em sua autobiografia, ele revelou sentir um profundo sentimento de tristeza por não se lembrar de ter trabalhado em uma história da qual gostava muito. A inspiração para criar Cujo veio da vida real. Em 1977, a Harley-Davidson de King quebrou em uma estrada de terra no Maine. Ele levou a motocicleta até o mecânico local, que ficava em uma área isolada. Ao chegar lá, King se surpreendeu ao ver o que considerou o maior cão da raça São Bernardo que já vira na vida. Além de rosnar de maneira agressiva para King, o animal ainda tentou avançar sobre ele. Felizmente, o mecânico apareceu e acalmou o animal, que viria a ser a principal fonte de inspiração para a obra Cujo. A adaptação cinematográfica foi lançada em 1983. Dee Wallace interpreta Donna Trenton, a mãe; Danny Pintauro, Tad Trenton, o filho de cinco anos; e Daniel Hugh Kelly, Vic Trenton, o pai. O maior destaque é a performance visceral de Denise Crosby ao lado do pequeno Danny Pintauro. Destaco também o excelente trabalho com os cães utilizados para interpretar Cujo, o personagem responsável por todo o terror da história, publicada originalmente em 1981. Em "Cujo", o espectador acompanha uma história de drama sobre traição, até que o terror e o suspense tomam conta da trama. O espectador fica apreensivo e imerso no desfecho daquela mãe desesperada, que luta pela própria sobrevivência e, principalmente, pela do filho. A sensação de desespero aumenta com cada aparição do enorme cão raivoso, nojento e implacável, que continua a atacar mesmo em estado de putrefação, devido à raiva transmitida pela mordida de um morcego. Assim, o espectador experimenta um pouco do desespero da mãe e do filho diante de um cenário caótico e isolado, no qual o interior do carro é a única proteção disponível. Acredito que, devido aos seus vícios na época em que escreveu o romance de terror Cujo, King tornou a história mais sombria ao dar um final trágico para a vida do pequeno Tad Trenton. Para "consertar" esse desfecho cruel, o estúdio optou por manter o menino vivo, considerando a morte da criança uma cena muito pesada. Essa mudança foi aprovada pelo próprio King, que admitiu se arrepender de ter matado a criança na história original. Se você está procurando um filme de terror repleto de suspense, que o prenda do início ao fim, o diretor Lewis Teague oferece exatamente isso em uma adaptação cinematográfica que merece ser vista — e até mesmo revisitada. Foi o que fiz antes de escrever esta resenha.

Pues, en la pelicula, no se presentan las emociones  y fuero interno de los personajes a fondo… como perciben el exterior. Cujo, que aterrador… Violento y gigantesco. Cujo is not really a film about a rabid dog. That is merely the skin it wears. Beneath the blood, the barking, the dust and the suffocating heat is something far more disturbing: the idea that sometimes there is no monster hiding in the darkness because the darkness has already found its way into the ordinary world. Cujo begins as something innocent. A massive, affectionate St. Bernard whose greatest crime is being a dog. Then a single bite changes everything. Rabies becomes the invisible hand reaching inside an innocent creature and turning love into instinct, loyalty into violence, and familiarity into terror. And that is what makes Cujo so fucking bleak. The dog isn't evil. There is no calculated hatred behind those eyes. No supernatural intelligence. No demonic possession. Just a living thing slowly being stripped of itself until instinct is all that remains. In a strange way, Cujo becomes a metaphor for what happens when something innocent is infected by something it never asked for. But the film doesn't stop there. Donna's crumbling marriage, Tad's childhood terror, Vic's absence, the neglected house, the oppressive summer heat everything feels like it is quietly decaying long before Cujo arrives. The dog is almost the physical manifestation of everything that has already gone wrong. And then comes the car. That fucking car becomes a coffin. Trapped inside it with her son, Donna is no longer fighting some cinematic creature that can conveniently be defeated. She's fighting exhaustion, dehydration, heat, panic and the terrifying knowledge that the thing outside only needs one mistake. The car becomes a tiny island of civilisation surrounded by something primitive. Inside: mother and child. Outside: hunger. And between them is nothing but glass. What makes the film particularly cruel is how little control its characters actually possess. There is no heroic cavalry riding over the horizon. No clever escape. No reassuring sense that the universe gives a shit whether these people survive. The world simply keeps moving. That is perhaps the darkest thing about Cujo. The horror isn't that evil exists. It's that sometimes suffering doesn't require evil at all. Sometimes tragedy is just biology, circumstance, bad timing and a series of tiny failures colliding at exactly the wrong moment. Cujo himself becomes almost tragic in the process. Somewhere beneath the blood and madness is the same dog who once wagged his tail and greeted people with affection. The creature attacking Donna is simultaneously the victim and the threat. And that makes him far more disturbing than a conventional monster. Because you can't hate him completely. You can only fear what he has become. The film's atmosphere feels like a fever dream dry, suffocating and increasingly claustrophobic. The heat isn't merely background scenery; it feels like another predator. Everything is baked, exhausted and dying. Even the silence seems to sweat. And Tad's fear gives the film another layer entirely. To a child, the world is already enormous and incomprehensible. A dark closet can become an abyss. A nightmare can become reality. Now imagine being trapped inside a car while something enormous and violent circles outside. The film understands something deeply uncomfortable about childhood: Children don't need to understand death to be terrified of it. They only need to understand that Mum might not be able to protect them. That is where Cujo sinks its teeth into something deeper than animal horror. It's about helplessness. About watching something you love deteriorate and being powerless to stop it. About the thin line separating civilisation from instinct. About how quickly the familiar can become alien. And ultimately, about survival. There is no grand philosophical explanation waiting at the end. No cosmic meaning behind what happens. Just people desperately trying to stay alive while the world closes around them. Cujo isn't frightening because he's a monster. He's frightening because he was never supposed to be one. He was someone's beloved dog. And perhaps that's the cruelest metaphor of all: Sometimes the thing that destroys you isn't born evil. Sometimes it is simply something innocent that has been infected, broken, starved, neglected or pushed beyond the point where it can recognise itself. Cujo leaves you with that uncomfortable thought long after the barking stops. The monster isn't always hiding under the bed. Sometimes it used to sleep beside you.

A mother and her young son find themselves ensnared in their immobilized vehicle during a heatwave, threatened by a once-gentle St. Bernard now driven insane by rabies. This taut, surprisingly character-driven adaptation of Stephen King’s novel is anchored by a powerful performance from Dee Wallace, who infuses real emotional depth into the role of a woman already grappling with domestic pressures before the horror unfolds. Danny Pintauro is equally compelling as her terrified son, providing the film with a genuine sense of vulnerability. Director Lewis Teague maintains a tight and grounded focus, prioritizing tension over spectacle. Charles Bernstein contributes an effective, unobtrusive score that subtly heightens the film’s mounting dread without calling attention to itself. The canine effects—a combination of trained animals and practical techniques—are executed with precision, and the film never loses sight of the tragedy underlying the menace. The final act is particularly strong, functioning like a pressure cooker that relies on performance and pacing rather than shock tactics. A lean, earnest thriller that transcends its “killer dog” premise due to dedicated acting and a straightforward, no-nonsense approach. It stands out as one of the more emotionally impactful King adaptations of its time.
